belief: I have sinned too much to be forgiven.
meta: A Christian look at the false belief that you have sinned too much to be forgiven, with Scripture, questions, and homework for replacing it with the truth.
origins: Years of the same struggle, with many failed promises to change. A long list of regrets that seems to grow every day. Being told “You should know better by now.” Picturing God keeping a running tally of every wrong. A parent or authority whose patience ran out quickly.
teaches: God does not keep a tally that eventually runs out. If He kept track of iniquities, no one could stand, but with Him there is forgiveness. His mercies are new every morning. Jesus told Peter to forgive not seven times, but seventy-seven times, showing the heart of God. When the prodigal son came home after wasting everything, his father ran to him and embraced him. The amount of your sin is never greater than the mercy of God.
self_statements: I’ve used up all my chances.
God must be tired of forgiving me.
I keep failing, so there’s no hope.
There’s a limit, and I’ve reached it.
I’ve sinned too many times to come back.
God forgives others, but my list is too long.
errors: Picturing God’s patience running out like a tired human parent’s.
Making the number of your sins look bigger than God’s mercy.
Predicting that God will refuse you next time.
Concluding “I feel hopeless, so I must be beyond help.”
Dismissing the promises that His mercies are new every morning.
questions: If God kept a list, could anyone stand before Him?
What does it mean that His mercies are new every morning?
How did the father treat the son who wasted everything?
If Jesus told us to forgive seventy-seven times, what does that say about God?
Who taught me that forgiveness has a limit?
Is my real problem too many sins, or not believing God’s mercy?
What would I do differently today if I believed I am forgiven?
truth: I have not sinned too much to be forgiven. God does not keep a tally that runs out. With Him there is forgiveness, and His mercies are new every morning. Like the father in the story of the prodigal son, God runs to meet me when I turn back to Him. His mercy is greater than all my sin.
hw_questions: If God kept a list, could anyone stand?
What does “new every morning” mean for me?
How did the father treat the prodigal son?
What does “seventy-seven times” say about God?
Who taught me forgiveness has a limit?
What would I do today if I believed I am forgiven?
hw_truths: His mercies are new every morning.
God runs to meet me when I turn back to Him.
God does not keep a tally that runs out.
God’s mercy is greater than all my sin.
When I return to God, He will freely pardon.
log: Each morning, write: “His mercies are new this morning,” and one thing I am starting fresh today.
name_example: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD, Sarah is not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
actions: and write down everything the father does when his son returns.
Each morning this week, start the day by saying,
“Today is a fresh start with God,” before checking your phone.
After a failure, confess it once, then do one helpful task
“Have you ever felt you had sinned too much? What helped?”
prayer: Merciful Father, thank You that with You there is forgiveness. Help me reject the lie that I have sinned too much to be forgiven. Thank You that Your mercies are new every morning and that You run to meet me when I come home. Help me receive Your mercy and begin again today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
songs: A reminder that God removes our sins completely, as far as east is from west, and does not keep them on file (Psalm 103:12).
An invitation to bring every failure to Jesus, because His blood covers the very sins we think are too much.
A song about God making something beautiful and clean out of a life that felt ruined.
Our past does not define us; in Christ we are redeemed, not condemned by the sins we keep replaying.
